subChunks.title: Defining & Calling Methods
subChunks.hookHtml: Suppose you copy-paste the same 10 lines of code in 5 different places. Then you discover a bug in those lines. How many places do you need to fix? Five. Methods solve this problem by letting you write code once and reuse it anywhere.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Methods: Named Incantations

A method is a named block of code that performs a specific task. You define it once, then call it by name whenever you need it.

A void method performs an action but returns no value:

public static void greet() {
    System.out.println("Welcome to Arcane Academy!");
}

public static void main(String[] args) {
    greet(); // call the method
    greet(); // call it again
}

The method signature consists of: access modifier (public), static (needed to call from main without creating an object), return type (void), method name, and parentheses for parameters.

To call a method: write its name followed by parentheses: greet();.

Methods promote DRY code — Don't Repeat Yourself.

storyBeats.text: Archmage Eldrin's grimoire is filled with named spells. Each page holds a complete incantation — ready to be cast the moment its name is spoken.

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: Every time you find yourself writing the same lines twice, stop and ask: should this be a named incantation? A method? Write it once, in one place, and summon it whenever needed.

storyBeats.speaker: A simple greeting method
Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: Three calls to greet() — three identical lines of output — yet the implementation is written only once. Change the message in one place, and all three calls update instantly. That is the power of methods!

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml: Create a static void method called printBanner() that prints === Welcome ===. Call it 3 times from main.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain what a method is, why we use them, and what the 'static' and 'void' keywords mean in a method signature.
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml: Without any starter code, write a complete class. Define a static void method called printSeparator() that prints ----------. In main, print Section 1, call printSeparator(), print Section 2, then call printSeparator() again.

questions.questionHtml: What return type should a method have if it performs an action but does NOT return a value?
questions.explanationHtml: void means the method returns nothing. It simply executes its statements and finishes.

questions.questionHtml: You can call the same method multiple times in a program.
questions.explanationHtml: That is the whole point of methods — define once, call as many times as needed. Each call executes the method body from top to bottom.
shout() is called twice, so HELLO! is printed twice on separate lines.

questions.questionHtml:
Complete the method signature to define a method with no parameters that returns nothing:
public ______ void sayHello() { ... }
questions.explanationHtml: The static keyword allows the method to be called from a static context (like main) without needing to create an object.

subChunks.title: Parameters & Return Values
subChunks.hookHtml: A spell that does the exact same thing regardless of what you feed it is not very useful. Real methods take input (parameters) and give back output (return values).
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Parameters & Return Values

Parameters are variables listed in the method signature. They act as inputs to the method. When you call the method, you pass arguments — the actual values — for each parameter.

public static void greet(String name) { // name is a parameter
    System.out.println("Hello, " + name + "!");
}

greet("Eldrin");  // "Eldrin" is the argument
greet("Alice");

A method can have multiple parameters, separated by commas:

public static void describe(String name, int level) {
    System.out.println(name + " is level " + level);
}

Return values — instead of void, specify the type the method will return, then use the return keyword to send a value back to the caller:

public static int add(int a, int b) {
    return a + b;
}

int result = add(3, 4); // result == 7
System.out.println(result);

The return statement also ends the method — no code after it in the same path runs.

storyBeats.text: Archmage Eldrin prepares a potion. He reaches for the ingredient shelf, pausing to explain.

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: A generic potion recipe is useless — you must specify the ingredients. In Java, those ingredients are called parameters. And every worthwhile recipe produces a result — a return value.

storyBeats.speaker: Method with parameters
Method with return value
Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: The parameter is the placeholder in the recipe: int potency. The argument is the actual ingredient you pass: 15. Master this distinction and your spells will always be flexible!

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
Write a static int add(int a, int b) method that returns the sum of a and b. In main, call it twice and print the results:

  • add(7, 5) → should print 12
  • add(100, 23) → should print 123
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain the difference between a parameter and an argument, and why return values make methods more useful.
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml: Without any starter code, write a class that defines a static double multiply(double a, double b) method returning the product of its two parameters. In main, call it with 3.5 and 4.0 and print the result. Expected output: 14.0.

questions.questionHtml: What is the term for the actual value you pass when calling a method?
questions.explanationHtml: The parameter is the placeholder in the method definition. The argument is the concrete value you provide when calling the method.

questions.questionHtml: A method declared with return type int must contain a return statement that returns an int.
questions.explanationHtml: If the return type is not void, the method must return a value of the declared type on every possible execution path, or the code will not compile.

questions.correctAnswer: The method declares return type int but has no return statement — add 'return result;'
questions.explanationHtml: A non-void method must return a value. The method computes result but never returns it. Add return result; (or return a * b;) before the closing brace.

subChunks.title: Method Overloading
subChunks.hookHtml: Can two methods share the same name? In Java, yes — as long as their parameter lists differ. This is called overloading, and it makes your API feel natural to use.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Method Overloading

Java allows multiple methods with the same name in the same class, provided they have different parameter types or counts. Java picks the right method at compile time based on what arguments you pass.

public static void greet(String name) {
    System.out.println("Hello, " + name + "!");
}

public static void greet(String name, int age) {
    System.out.println("Hello, " + name + "! You are " + age + ".");
}

greet("Alice");       // calls the 1-parameter version
greet("Bob", 25);   // calls the 2-parameter version

Overloading is NOT about return type. You cannot overload two methods that differ only in return type — Java would not know which to call and will refuse to compile.

You have already seen overloading: System.out.println() is overloaded to accept int, String, double, and more — all the same name!

storyBeats.text: Deep in the Academy's vault, Archmage Eldrin opens three matching vials, each labelled 'Fireball'.

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: The Academy's three Fireball incantations share a name — yet each differs by what you provide. A small fireball needs only a target. A medium one needs a target and intensity. The grand fireball needs all three. Java will choose the right one automatically.

storyBeats.speaker: Three Fireball overloads
Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: The compiler is the academy registrar — it matches your call to the correct overload by examining exactly what you pass. This is why you cannot distinguish overloads by return type alone: the registrar cannot see the return type at the call site!

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
Define three overloaded versions of a method called describe:

  1. describe(String name) — prints Name: Alice
  2. describe(String name, int age) — prints Name: Bob, Age: 25
  3. describe(String name, int age, String role) — prints Name: Carol, Age: 30, Role: Engineer

Call all three from main with the values shown.

guidedPracticeTests.label: All three overloads
guidedPracticeTests.expected:
Name: Alice
Name: Bob, Age: 25
Name: Carol, Age: 30, Role: Engineer

subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain method overloading: what it is, how Java decides which overload to call, and why you cannot overload based on return type alone.
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml: Without any starter code, write a class with an overloaded method called area: one version takes a single int side (square area = side × side), another takes int width and int height (rectangle area). Call both from main with values of your choice and print each result.

questions.questionHtml: What makes two methods with the same name valid overloads in Java?
options: They have different parameter lists (types or counts)
One is private, the other public
questions.correctAnswer: They have different parameter lists (types or counts)
questions.explanationHtml: Overloading is determined by the parameter signature. The return type is irrelevant — Java looks at the types and number of parameters to choose the overload.

questions.questionHtml: Which method is called and what is printed?
questions.explanationHtml: The literal 5 is an int, so Java picks the show(int) overload.

questions.questionHtml: You can create two methods with the same name and same parameters if they have different return types.
questions.explanationHtml: Return type is not part of the method signature for overloading purposes. Two methods with the same name and same parameter list are always ambiguous — the code will not compile.

subChunks.title: Scope & Variable Lifetime
subChunks.hookHtml: Why can't you use a variable declared inside an if block once you exit it? The answer is scope — every variable only lives within the curly braces where it was born.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Variable Scope

Scope is the region of code where a variable is accessible. In Java, scope is determined by curly braces { }:

  • Local scope — a variable declared inside a method or block lives only until its closing }
  • Block scope — variables inside if, for, or while blocks are invisible outside them
  • Parameter scope — method parameters are local to the method body
public static void example() {
    int outer = 10;
    if (true) {
        int inner = 20;
        System.out.println(outer); // OK — outer is in scope
        System.out.println(inner); // OK — inner is in scope here
    }
    System.out.println(outer); // OK
    // System.out.println(inner); // ERROR — inner is out of scope!
}

Shadowing — if you declare a variable with the same name in an inner scope, it temporarily hides the outer one. This is legal but can be confusing; avoid it when possible.

storyBeats.text: Archmage Eldrin leads the apprentice through the Academy's winding corridors. Each room has its own slate board covered in glowing runes.

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: Every room in the Academy has its own rune board. Runes inscribed in the alchemy lab cannot be read from the library — they exist only within that room's walls. In Java, every pair of curly braces is such a room.

storyBeats.speaker: Scope of rooms (blocks)
Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: You can read a rune from any room you can reach from where the rune was inscribed — including inner rooms. But once you leave the lab, the lab's runes vanish.

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
Write a program that demonstrates scope. Declare int outer = 10 in the method. Inside an if (true) block, declare int inner = 20 and print it. After the block, print outer again.

Expected output:

Outer: 10
Inner: 20
10
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain variable scope in Java using a real-world analogy, describing what happens when you try to use a variable outside its scope.
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml: Without any starter code, demonstrate scope: declare int total = 0 before a for loop that runs from 1 to 5. Inside each iteration, declare int step = i * 2 and add it to total. After the loop, print total. Expected output: 30.

questions.questionHtml: Where can a variable declared inside a for loop be accessed?
options: Only inside the for loop's body
Only on the line it is declared
questions.correctAnswer: Only inside the for loop's body
questions.explanationHtml: A variable declared in a for loop header or body is scoped to that loop. It cannot be accessed before the loop or after it closes.

questions.correctAnswer: x is declared inside the if block and cannot be accessed outside it — declare x before the if block
questions.explanationHtml: x is scoped to the if block. Move the declaration before the if block to make it accessible after it closes.

questions.questionHtml: A method parameter can be accessed anywhere in the class, not just inside the method.
questions.explanationHtml: Method parameters have local scope — they exist only within the method body. They are destroyed when the method returns.

questions.questionHtml: Two variables are declared: int x = 1 in the method and int x = 2 inside a nested block. What happens?
options: The inner x shadows the outer x inside the block
Both variables are merged into one
The outer x is permanently overwritten
questions.correctAnswer: The inner x shadows the outer x inside the block
questions.explanationHtml: This is called shadowing. Inside the inner block, x refers to the inner variable. Outside the block, x refers to the outer one. Legal but confusing — avoid when possible.
